n: The father asks his son not just to remember his teaching but to keep it in his heart—obedience that comes from within.

f.g: Hebrew torah—teaching or instruction, here a parent’s guidance.

n: Living by wise teaching tends to bring long life and peace. Proverbs states general principles of how life usually works, not guarantees for every case.

f.g: Hebrew shalom—wholeness and well-being, not just absence of conflict.

n: Keep loyal love and faithfulness close: wear them like a necklace and write them on your heart like a tablet. The image recalls the law written on stone, now written inward.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed and ʾemet—steadfast covenant love and faithfulness.
table = tablet, a writing surface.

n: The result is a good reputation with both God and people—just as was said of the boy Jesus.

f.w: in the sight of God and man

n: One of the best-loved verses in the Bible. Rely on the Lord completely, rather than relying only on your own limited judgment.

f.w: Trust in the LORD with all thine heart

f.g: Do not prop yourself up on; don’t put your full weight on.

n: Recognize God in every part of life, and he will make your road straight—clearing the way and guiding you to the right destination.

f.g: Literally “know him”—stay aware of him and seek his will.
Or “make your paths straight.”

n: Don’t be impressed with your own cleverness. Humility before God and turning from evil are the start of real wisdom.

f.w: Be not wise in thine own eyes

n: Humble obedience is pictured as medicine for the body—healing to the core and refreshment to the bones.

f.g: Likely “body” or “flesh” in the original; the core of one’s physical self.

n: Honor God with your possessions, giving him the first and best of what you earn. Firstfruits were the first part of a harvest offered to the Lord.

f.g: substance = wealth, possessions.

n: The promise attached to generous giving: overflowing barns and wine vats. Latter-day Saints often connect this with blessings promised for tithing.

f.g: Winepresses or vats where grape juice was collected.

n: Don’t resent the Lord’s discipline or grow tired of his correction. Hard experiences can be part of God’s training.

f.g: chastening = discipline, corrective training.

f.w: despise not the chastening of the LORD

n: God disciplines because he loves, like a father who delights in his son. The book of Hebrews quotes this to comfort struggling believers.

f.w: whom the LORD loveth he correcteth

n: A new section praises wisdom itself. “Happy” here means truly blessed or fortunate.

f.g: Hebrew ʾashre—blessed, fortunate; the same word that opens Psalm 1.

n: Wisdom is a better investment than silver or gold. Its profits last.

f.w: better than the merchandise of silver

n: Wisdom is more precious than rubies (or red corals)—nothing you could want compares to her.

f.g: Possibly red coral or pearls; the exact gem is uncertain, but it means something very costly.

n: Wisdom is pictured as a woman offering gifts in both hands: long life in one, riches and honor in the other.

f.w: Length of days is in her right hand

n: Wisdom’s roads are pleasant and all her paths lead to peace.
Wisdom is a tree of life—recalling the tree in Eden. Latter-day Saints may think of Lehi’s vision, where the tree of life represents the love of God.
God used wisdom to found the earth and set the heavens in place. Chapter 8 will expand this picture of wisdom present at the Creation.

f.w: The LORD by wisdom hath founded the earth

n: By God’s knowledge the deep waters burst forth and the skies give dew—water above and below sustains life.

f.g: In dry Israel, dew was a vital source of moisture for crops.

n: Keep wisdom and good judgment in view; don’t let them slip out of sight.

f.g: Practical, effective wisdom.

n: Wisdom gives life to the soul and is like a beautiful ornament around the neck.
With wisdom you walk safely and don’t trip—a picture of a steady, secure life.
Wisdom brings peace even at night: you lie down unafraid and sleep well.
Don’t panic at sudden terror or at the ruin that comes on the wicked.
The secret of fearlessness is the Lord himself: he is your confidence and keeps your foot out of the hunter’s snare.

f.g: Caught in a trap, like an animal in a snare.

f.w: the LORD shall be thy confidence

n: Practical neighborly duties begin here. If you can help someone who deserves it, do it. Withholding good is a real wrong.
Don’t put off a neighbor with “come back tomorrow” when you can help today. Delay can be a form of unkindness.
Don’t plot harm against a neighbor who trusts you and lives peacefully beside you. Betraying trust is especially wicked.
Don’t pick fights with someone who has done you no wrong.

f.g: strive = quarrel, contend, bring a dispute.

n: Don’t envy violent people, even when they seem to succeed, and don’t copy their methods.
The Lord detests the devious, but he shares his confidence with the upright—his “secret” means close friendship and counsel.

f.w: his secret is with the righteous
f.g: secret = intimate counsel, close fellowship.
abomination = something God finds detestable.

n: A contrast of two homes: the house of the wicked lies under the Lord’s curse; the home of the righteous is blessed.

f.g: habitation = dwelling, home.

n: God mocks the mockers but gives grace to the humble. Both James and Peter quote this verse (from the Greek Old Testament).

f.w: he giveth grace unto the lowly

n: The wise will inherit honor; fools only get “promoted” to disgrace. The chapter ends contrasting two outcomes.
